It's hard to get qualified There's basically two routes: A) Getting an apprenticeship B) Paying for a Level 2/Level 3 diploma, then getting some work to complete the NVQ.

Apprenticeships are very competitive to get, and are suited towards school leavers. Apprenticeship starts have been falling: https://jtltraining.com/news/uk-falling-thousands-short-of-electricians-from-workforce-as-numbers-stand-still/

The diploma and NVQ courses are expensive, probably a minimum of £7000, and the total to get qualified can be over £9000. The NVQ requires you to be working, and as an unqualified electrician, you can only really be an electrician's mate. There is little work available for electricians mates, and where there is work, you are expected to know how to do the job already.

The training courses are in a classroom, which doesn't teach most of the actual job. In a domestic job, you may be crawling around a loft, or crawling around under a floor to get a cable from a to b. You might be drilling through joists, or chiseling out brick or block. It's noisy, dusty, hard physical work.

In commercial / industrial jobs, you may be crawling under a floor, climbing in and out of man holes, working at height, cutting tray / ladder or pulling heavy armoured cables. It can be very repetitive, and it's noisy, hard physical work. As a subcontractor, hours could be 7AM-5PM, so if you're an hour away, you'll spend 2 hours driving and 10 hours on site, which is a very long and tiring day. The people on site are probably people who did an apprenticeship as a school leaver, so they might not have much in common with you.

text:
Hi, I built Quaesito, a self-hosted quiz-night app for playing with friends. I thought it might be useful to others, so I wanted to share it here: https://github.com/ggirelli/quaesito

It runs on your laptop, which you can cast or screen-share on to a TV. Friends then connect and answer from their phones, as long as everyone is on the same local network. It support Windows, macOS, and Linux, although I have only tested it on Linux so far, so feedback on the other platforms would be very welcome.

I was especially careful to make it work over your local network. No requests are sent to third-party services.

I wanted something that made quiz nights more fun than just a slideshow or a PDF, with support for different types of question formats and multimedia. I have plenty of ideas for additional formats, but I wanted to keep the first release manageable.

The project was built entirely through vibe-coding, using Claude Code in an iterative process. I have released it under the MIT license and would appreciate any feedback, particularly from people who try running an actual quiz night with it.

Hope you find it useful, and have as much fun with it as I have!

Original post from my blog: https://ggirelli.info/blog/2026/10/11/quaesito

I also thought that, and then I started pointing Claude at various projects and having it look for optimizations. The projects themselves were, of course, largely AI-generated. What I found was that simply asking it to improve performance could indeed help, but if I pointed out specific architectural issues - like storing massive graphs in a giant JSON blob - and then recommended a solution (normalize, store in SQLite, recursive CTEs to walk it), the performance ceiling went WAY up.

Now, you could argue that AI didn’t fix that, I told it what to fix, and it just wrote the code. That’s valid, I suppose. The view I’m coming around to is that LLMs do know how to write performant code, but their corpus is so full of garbage that you have to tell it explicitly what you want, which requires you to know how to spot the problems and solve them.

I will not make any claims that they can write kernels or compilers well, because I haven’t tried to do either of those, on my own or with an LLM.

Another anecdote: yesterday, I got tired of dealing with Mumble on my LAN (random audio issues on the Mac clients, poor echo cancellation, etc.) and asked Claude to build a replacement. I gave it a rough spec, including non-goals (private use only, so no encryption needed, and I don’t care about supporting a large number of clients), then told it to build it in Rust, supporting MacOS and Windows both natively. Two hours later, it worked. Not just kind of, it worked flawlessly on Macs and Windows, and the audio quality and echo cancellation was perfect. The only bug I found - which it fixed - was denormal numbers was causing relatively high CPU (~1/2 of a core) usage on Windows due to x86_64 handling of that. The binary is 5 MB. It ran its own echo cancellation training while writing it to tune parameters. It implemented RFC 2198 without me mentioning it (hell, I didn’t even know about it - it’s fascinating!). When I fed it back some logs, it saw that one client had higher latency than expected (meshed WiFi without a backhaul), and then proceeded to create a network simulator so it could test various latency and jitter scenarios to solve it. While doing so, it also determined that Windows was lying about its latency numbers by 25 msec, and addressed that.

So again, I think LLMs are capable of excellent work, you just have to know what you need to ask for.

With WhatsApp, Discord, etc, that server is provided by Facebook, Discard respectively. With XMPP, Matrix, that server is the instance in which you have an account or where the channel is hosted.

With IRC, you use a bouncer. What makes IRC unique is that a bouncer is _optional_. You can even join a channel without an account and without a server which keeps logs while you're offline. This ephemeral level of joining doesn't exist in WhatsApp, Discord, XMPP, Matrix, etc.

And, btw, this is not a new thing: I first saw bouncers 15 years ago and they weren't even new back then.
